The cap price implies a P/E of ~19.6 versus a document benchmark of 70.6, which could attract late buying, but the gap is so wide it invites the question of whether the price band or the benchmark is the outlier.

longterm_view.reasoning: Revenue compounded ~17% over two years but EBITDA margin has been volatile and thin (7.0% → 4.5% → 5.4%), and the latest year's growth slowed to ~6% while total debt quadrupled to roughly ₹17.4bn (D/E 0.96 from 0.35) [figures: balance sheet]. This looks like a working-capital-hungry government/PSU contracting business [business, page 214] where rising bank guarantees (₹745cr given at FY26 vs ₹402cr at FY24) [promoters, page 329] signal the incremental borrowing is funding the contract bid machine, not de-risking the P&L.

governance.reasoning: Related-party transactions and guarantees are disclosed and cross-referenced [promoters, page 330, page 348], and the extracts flag no regulatory action [litigation, page 387]; but the guarantees outstanding have nearly doubled in two years, which is the only hard signal I have and it points the wrong way.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Debt rose ~3.6x in one year while guarantees given rose ~37%; in a PBG-driven contracting business this means growth is being bought with the balance sheet, and a working-capital squeeze could halt bidding [business, page 212; promoters, page 329].
A significant share of projects are Government/PSU, so receivables, order timing and margins depend on state budgets and payment cycles the company does not control [business, page 214].

The document itself warns that failure to maintain margins for PBGs means losing the ability to win new work — a circular dependency on lender goodwill with debt already near 1x equity [business, page 212].
At ~5% EBITDA margin, a single mispriced government contract or collection delay can erase a year's profit growth [figures: ebitda_margin_pct].
